unit-m3u1.title: Unit 3 · Lesson 1: Multiply by Powers of 10
unit-m3u1.source: enVision Topic 3 textbook scan — Multiply Multi-Digit Whole Numbers (Drive)

summary.text: Lesson 3-1 of the Topic 3 textbook scan: patterns for multiplying a whole number by 10, 100, 1,000 and so on, written in standard form and with exponents.

why.text: Every later lesson in this unit leans on this one — estimating, partial products and the standard algorithm all multiply by tens and hundreds.

objectives.text: Multiply a whole number by a power of 10 using patterns
Read and write powers of 10 with exponents
Count the zeros in both factors, including zeros already in the first number

parentNote.text: Two traps get their own card and question. The first is the one the textbook itself names: 60 × 1,000 is 60,000, not 6,000, because the zero already in 60 counts too. The second is treating an exponent as an ordinary factor — reading 10³ as 30. Both have a wrong option built from exactly that mistake, so if she picks one the explanation names it.

nextUp.text: Count the zeros in both numbers. That is the whole trick.

cards.def:
**1; 10; 100; 1,000; 10,000; 100,000 — each one is 10 times the one before it.**
• Every place in a number is worth 10 times the place to its right.
cards.hint: Each step left on the place-value chart is one more 10.

cards.def:
**10⁴ means 10 × 10 × 10 × 10, which is 10,000.**
• The small raised number is the exponent. It counts how many 10s are multiplied.
• It also tells you how many zeros the power of 10 has.

**The product ends with the zeros of the number PLUS the zeros of the power of 10.**
• 58 × 1,000 = 58,000.
• 58 × 10⁴ = 580,000.
cards.hint: Count the zeros in both factors, then write them all at the end.

cards.def:
**A zero inside the first factor still counts: 60 × 1,000 = 60,000, not 6,000.**
• 60 already ends in one zero, and 1,000 adds three more — four zeros in all.
cards.hint: Count every zero, including the one the number brought with it.

cards.term: An exponent is not a multiplier
cards.def:
**10³ is 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000. It is NOT 10 × 3 = 30.**
• The exponent says how many times 10 is used as a factor.
cards.hint: Three tens multiplied, not three tens added.

steps: Multiplying by 1,000 puts three zeros on the end of 47.

ex.main: **47,000.** Multiplying by 1,000 moves every digit three places to the left, which shows up as three zeros on the end.
ex.tip: 4,700 has only two zeros added — that is 47 × 100.

questions.q: What is 10⁴ written in standard form?
questions.hint: The exponent tells how many 10s are multiplied together.

ex.main: **10,000.** Four 10s multiplied together give a 1 followed by four zeros.
ex.tip: 40 is what you get if you multiply 10 by 4 — the exponent does not work that way.

questions.hint: Count the zeros in BOTH numbers.
steps: Together that is three zeros after the 7.

ex.main: **7,000.** The zero in 70 counts too, so the product ends in three zeros, not two.
ex.tip: Forgetting the zero that 70 already has is the most common slip here.

ex.main: **26,000.** The exponent 3 means 1,000, so three zeros go on the end of 26.
ex.tip: 78 is 26 × 3 — treating the exponent as an ordinary factor.

questions.hint: How many zeros were added to 58 to make 580,000?
steps: Four added zeros means multiplying by 10,000.

ex.main: **10⁴.** 580,000 is 58 with four zeros added, and 10⁴ is the power of 10 with four zeros.
ex.tip: Count only the zeros that were ADDED to 58 — the digits 5 and 8 are not zeros.

questions.hint: 10³ adds three zeros. How many zeros are left over in 90,000?
steps: One zero must come from the missing number, so it is 90.

ex.main: **90.** 90 × 1,000 = 90,000 — one zero from 90 and three from 10³.
ex.tip: 9 × 10³ is only 9,000. Check by multiplying your answer back.

questions.q: A team gives a cap to each of the first 100 fans through the gate. Each cap costs $17. How much do the caps cost in all?
questions.hint: Multiply the cost of one cap by the number of caps.

ex.main: **$1,700.** 17 × 100 = 1,700, because multiplying by 100 adds two zeros.
ex.tip: $117 comes from adding 100 and 17 — but "each" means multiply.

questions.q: Without multiplying, which is greater: 64 × 10³ or 7 × 10⁴?
opts: 64 × 10³, because it has more digits to start with
They are equal, because both use a power of 10
questions.hint: Rewrite both as standard numbers by counting zeros.

ex.main: **7 × 10⁴.** The bigger power of 10 outweighs the bigger first factor: 70,000 beats 64,000.
ex.tip: Comparing only the first factors ignores the part that makes the biggest difference.

questions.q: Theo says 40 × 1,000 = 4,000 because 1,000 has three zeros. What went wrong?
opts: He forgot the zero already in 40, so it is 40,000
He should have added the numbers, so it is 1,040
He added one zero too many, so it is 400
questions.hint: Count the zeros in both factors.
steps: 40 has one zero of its own.
That makes four zeros after the 4: 40,000.

ex.main: **He forgot the zero already in 40.** Four zeros in all, so the product is 40,000.
ex.tip: This is the trap the textbook itself names — every zero counts, including the ones in the first number.

questions.q: Which is the same as multiplying a number by 10³?
steps: Multiplying by 10³ is multiplying by 10, then 10, then 10.
That is multiplying by 10 three times.

ex.main: **Multiplying it by 10 three times.** The exponent counts how many 10s are factors.
ex.tip: Adding 10 three times only adds 30 — nowhere near multiplying by 1,000.
